title: Evaluation and Release Gating
subtitle: Design one shared gate that passes, blocks or holds prompt and model changes for 30 AI applications, without letting a strong average hide a failing critical slice.
author: By Sourav Banerjee

practice_prompts.label: Restate the ask and discovery
practice_prompts.hint: Turn the dashboard request into a release decision, name the four stakeholders and the questions that change the design.

practice_prompts.label: Sizing and architecture
practice_prompts.hint: Size against the release window and trace one candidate through the control and data planes.

practice_prompts.label: Gate logic, slices and graders
practice_prompts.hint: State the four checks, block versus hold, slice minimums and how the grader earns trust.

practice_prompts.label: Incident, rollout and cost
practice_prompts.hint: Explain how the gate catches the sales-copilot regression, how it rolls out, and how you cut the eval bill.

rubric: Restates the ask as a pass/block/hold decision with an owner, threshold and record, not a dashboard.
Sizes 3M executions and 6-15M calls a day against a six-hour window, not the daily average.
Separates the control plane from the sandboxed data plane and reads only validated results.
Compares Δ against a pinned baseline on four separate dimensions, judging quality on a lower bound and safety on a floor.
Distinguishes missing evidence (block) from thin evidence (hold) and never passes by default.
Requires each critical slice to pass with a minimum size, citing the 96.7% / 83.3% sales-copilot incident.
Calibrates the versioned LLM grader against humans and keeps it advisory until agreement holds.
Cuts eval cost by tiering and judge routing without thinning critical slices.

editorial_review.evidence: Built the inventory from all 49 captured sections, splitting the dense Full Design parts (sections 1-14) into 86 teaching items. Interview Guide, Deep Dive, Cheat Sheet and Full Design repeat the gate four times; I consolidated them so each mechanism is taught once in walkthrough steps 1-12 or a deep dive, then recalled in Quick review, and checked each repeat for a distinct number or caveat before merging (e.g. the deep-dive 'pre-headroom' qualifier and the 'severe escape becomes incident case' rule only appear once in the source and were kept). Added plain definitions (candidate, baseline, slice, p95, MoSCoW, fail closed, ETag, circuit breaker, weak supervision), a refund-bot trace and an illustrative bootstrap lower-bound explanation, labelled as such; the old minute plan's section numbers were rewritten as links. The upgrade plan is taught as nine steps. The source worksheet page was not captured and is linked rather than imported. Source inconsistencies resolved in text (2026-11-16): the upgrade-regression plan was labelled 'eleven steps' but lists nine actions → the casebook says 'nine steps' and lists the nine, because no other source section supplies two more steps. November 20 complete maintained-baseline review: Complete maintained casebook: brief, twelve walkthrough steps, five diagrams, records and API, decision code and test, lower-bound statistics, sales-copilot incident, neighbouring prompts, threat model, cost pivot, all practice reveals and Quick review.
